title: Offensive Coordinator Bobby Slowik meets with the media | Miami Dolphins
text: uh some chatter from fans about the third day play to Bell and Malik not saying he covered Coleman. He was asked about it yesterday. Should he have seen Coleman on that play and thrown to him instead? >> Uh the I mean that play is critical moment of the game, right? We're expecting cover zero. We got cover zero. We put a play in specifically for cover zero. We got exactly what we want. We got an allout blitz. Uh we have two posts on the left. We have a stick on the right. And the way we equip our quarterback in in this system is is we want to give them options like if our pockets not good if maybe we don't pick things up the way we want. We have an outlet to the right on a stick uh that we can throw and is always available to him to throw. Like the way we coach and especially when you get a cover zero team like you want to be aggressive against cover zero and you have two posts on the play and I think Malik's mindset on that was I'm going to be aggressive and honestly it was a ball that is a 50/50 ball that I would expect and I think our offense would expect we come down with a 100 times out of a hundred and I think Chris Bell would say the same thing. So um I think it's easy after the fact for everybody to go through like well could we have done this could we have done that? Um, but really I think ultimately the play came down like it's it's in football it's so funny. It's a trickle down to everything, right? You we put in a special protection to pick up an allout blitz against the defense that's probably the best in the NFL at doing allout blitzes. We pick it all up, but we're a hair off on when the on the balls being snapped like a hair early. Now Will's a little out of position. He picks off AJ. Will gets edge. AJ gets edge. Now the pocket's not clean. Now it's not, you know, so it's like all these things add together on it. um which is you know why the detail of everything we do right now with our team is so important all the way across the board. >> So that's not viewed as a negative play for him when you go back and look at the tape. >> No for Malik. Okay. And then there was one other play where obviously Coleman in the corner of the end zone was a very narrow window for him to get the ball. Looked like Malik at least from the TV copy was streaking open late in that play. I don't know if you saw that. Was there an opportunity to go to Malik there? And in general, I guess, has Malik Willis been not seeing open receivers or has that not been an issue? >> Yeah, I I think Malik Willis is doing just fine. I think you have a quarterback that excels in off schedule and athleticism and I think he's shown that through the course of four games. I think he's still getting used to the system that we're running when we're talking about playing in the pocket. We've gotten better at getting rid of the ball fast. Um, but it's something he's still always gonna gonna continue to work on as we go through the season because again, this is a new scheme for him. I think anytime you sit there and even as a coach, you you use a clicker and you rewind a play six times and you start to question the decision of somebody that I think is doing the hardest thing in the world in sports, in quarterback, uh, I I think you're getting into a really dangerous game. And you know what I ask of him is we stick to what it is we teach. We go through the process of what it is we teach and then whatever you decide to do, you do it aggressive and you do it convicted. And if you do that, we're going to be happy with with what you decide. You know, you're too talented not to go make really good plays. So, um you know, I think Malik is taking steps in that direction every day. Every day I see him in practice getting better every game. I think he's taking steps to get better as well. >> How do you see the running backs respond? How did you see the running backs respond following a chance injury? >> Uh, yeah, I thought they I thought they both stepped up. You know, I it it was one of those games where when Ali was in, a lot of the runs he had, you know, were were the right runs and he took advantage of them, you know, and he made some big plays. He made a big play on third down to get us down the red area and then he, you know, obviously scored and had some big runs on the way. Um, and I I I really think Jay Wright actually ran pretty well, too. He it was like he had the opposite. It was the other side of the coin. You know, he had some really tough run looks and it works out sometimes that way. uh when you have multiple backs that are kind of doing it by committee. Sometimes a guy just gets the rough share and somebody gets the good share and and um but I still thought Jay Wright took some runs that were maybe three, four yard gains and he was able to run for five, six, seven, one, he was able to run for eight, keep us on schedule and then he had the one on third and two where I mean there's there's you know there's just not much you can do um when we execute it that way. So, um, I thought both of them really like as far as carrying the ball, I thought they stepped up. Um, and I was equally proud of of Ali in the third down stuff. You know, protections was something that he's been doing, but we really put a lot on his plate on third down this past game. Like, that's a really hard defense as far as protections go in situational football. Uh, and I thought our protection throughout the game is credit to the O line and to the backs. Like I thought our protection was was really good against a tough defense to have good protection against. So I I I was really pleased with both of them. >> Follow up. Yeah. Just does Halfley prefer to ride the hot hand or um stay committed to the committee is or is that better question for him tomorrow? >> Yeah, I mean it's probably a better question for him tomorrow. You know, I I would say my feeling on it is uh you know, I think eventually through every game, you wind up getting a feel for the guys and and if one guy maybe is hotter than the other, you're going to have them out there more, you're still going to wind up splitting time. Like guys are especially here in Miami, like they're going to get tired, you know? Um early in the game, I probably lean more towards like, let's stick with the plan and and let's see how this plays out because it could just be a onewrun thing that's blocked really well, you know. Um, so I think there's some feel there and and ultimately that's coach Halfley's decision, so that's probably good one for him. >> You said that it was the right run for Oie a lot of the times. Are you referring to like his decision-making on that? What does that reference to? >> Uh, I mean, it could reference a lot of things. I'd say first thing it always references is the play call. Did I actually have a decent play call? Um, and then secondly, you know, how how we block it. You know, did we block this well? Are we blocking it the way we envisioned it being blocked? Is the window that we want to hit the anticipated window or is he going to have to make something happen that maybe we didn't anticipate happening? Um, you know, like all those things kind of together can make a running back have a really good day or a really tough long day, you know, so there's a lot that goes into it. Like everything in football, there's 11 guys on the field and you need all 11 to roll. >> It's a great answer into my question I wanted to ask originally, which is four games into the season, you guys have a very diverse run scheme with multiple different types of running plays. Do you anticipate that continuing? Is that your goal to continue that? Or as the season goes on, do you try to hone in on the things that you do especially well and try to maybe narrow it down to more of that? How do you balance being diverse in the running game, but also maybe sticking to what you do best? >> Yeah, I I think that's something we're all kind of figuring out right now, you know, all the way across the offense. Um, you know, I think every every week you go into it like, how do I help this individual all the way across the board at every position? And then once you go beyond the individual, how do I help our unit succeed and you evaluate that always starting as a coordinator and play caller and then you go as coaches and then you go to players. But um I think right now we're kind of in the boat like all right, where's where's the sweet spot for us? Um are we maybe are we like are we doing too much where we got to cut stuff back? Uh are we not doing enough and we have to add more to help these guys get in more advantageous positions? you know, I think it's it's constantly like fluctuating and then you add in, well, what are we going against? Is this something we're going to be able to ID and know or is this way complex and there's a lot of pieces? So, it's it's like constantly changing. I would say overall my mentality in the run game is I want to make the simple look complex, you know, like I I I think from our perspective right now, we we probably don't do as much as people would think we do, which in that case, we're I'm doing my job. Um but if we give the illusion of complexity then I think we're in a good spot. and sticking to Ali um obviously because we have seen what he can do on the field but al also we've gotten to know him over the past few weeks and we know that he has such a charismatic personality right so when his number gets called after what happened with a uh what does it mean to have a guy that not only can be explosive on the field but also in the locker room right uh just trying to become that leader uh what does that bring to the room and to the offense in general >> he's just got energy and he's got a lot of juice uh every day, all the time, you know, um which it's a lot of fun like when you have someone that's like that day in day out on the practice field, in the locker room, in the meeting rooms, um you know, when when you're in games and you're trying to overcome something, you can rely on his energy to be there. When you're in a game and something good happens, you can rely on his energy to keep it going, you know? So, uh that part of it is just really fun. Uh it's a joy to be around. It's also like you also know when Ali maybe isn't isn't having Ali's best day, you know what I mean? Because his energy level is so consistent. As soon as you see a little dip, you're like, "Whoa, man. Like, what's what's going on?" You know, and then boom, he's back. Um, so I I just I've had fun seeing him last year as a rookie, see what he went through, what he battled through, just the general rookie process to where he is now, continuing to grow. And going into this year, he wasn't getting a whole lot of reps through camp and preeason. And to see him, you know, be mature and and handle it the right way and really still work his tail off and then to have a game like he had, like I'm just really happy for him. >> What would be a key against Dexter Lawrence? >> Yeah, Dexter Lawrence is difficult man to block, right? I mean, he's he's I I swear to you, I feel like sometimes as a nose he'll align and I think he occupies two gaps. I mean, he's just huge. So, I would say for us, I think uh one thing that helps us is is we can count on Brewer an awful lot. Like I I'm not ever saying like our game plan is going in Brewer, you got Dexter one-on-one all game, man. You know what I mean? Like we wouldn't do that. But obviously Brewer is one of our best players. Uh so to be able to have one of our best players near one of their best players is helpful for us. Um but he's just he's tough because he impacts a run game a great deal. They got a really good run defense. I think they're ranked like top five or something like that. Um, and then obviously that he's a really good pass rusher. Like he's a disruptor on the interior as a pass rusher. And that's that's normally a three technique spot. And when it comes from the shade, that gets way harder to help and handle in protections, I think, than than people realize because it's really rare. Um, so that that for us, that's a huge challenge. like we're going to have some stuff in the run game where we know, okay, how can we just help in protections? I think it's it's going to be really big. I mean, they're they're good all the way across the front and pass rush us. They blitz less, I think, than anyone else in the NFL. They're still somewhere third in sacks or something like that. Like their D line is their D line is good. It's a good challenge for us up front. It's good challenge for our O line. It's a good challenge for Brewer because that's who he's going to be lined up against most of the game. you gone to maintain the identity of wanting to run the football and to see it come to fruition with Ali's 100 yard game. >> Yeah, I mean I I think you know it's still every time I just think about losing Devon, my heart hurts for him because I I was really I think everybody was just so fired up and happy with where he was as as a player and especially where he was going as a leader um and how he was helping our whole unit. Uh, I would say the what made him, you know, obviously he's got home run ability. He's a heck of a running back, but the his skills that like not a lot of other backs in the league have is his receiving ability. And I think we felt that through the first three weeks. Uh, and I would say, you know, I think his receiving ability is special. Outside of that, I don't really think our identity has changed. You know, like we came into this wanting to be a tough, physical team that played with high effort. Like that's who we want to be. Uh that's what we want to be every every day, every game. Um and that identity isn't going to change uh because Devon's not here. Like we have Jay Wright and Ali here and and Carlos and Quz here because that's the identity we want to be. So we have people here that we know can continue that identity. So that part of it isn't going to be any different. Um but it it was, you know, the first half was tough sledding in the run game. Really all the way around the board. I would say on offense it it was not a good first half. I was really pleased with how guys responded in the second half and in the run game in particular. I thought in the second half we ran the ball really really well.

title: Sam Darnold On Preparing For Week 5, Offense's Progress Through Four Games | Seattle Seahawks
text: Good.  Good.  Yes, we've been, you know, pretty productive these past few days. Of course, we are preparing for a meeting with a very strong 49ers team .  So we are doing everything we can to prepare for Sunday and secure the best position for ourselves. I think their defense is the best in the league at containing explosive attacks.  What exactly do you think makes them so good at this? Yeah, you know, they're doing really well.  I think if you dig into the details, their linebackers, defensive backs, and defensive line work very well together.  They do a great job of keeping the game in front of them and are very good at capturing players, which I think helps minimize explosive moments. You are playing against a team that limits such attacks.  How do you find a balance between being aggressive so they don't take the initiative and taking what they give you? I think as a quarterback, you always want to stick to the plan, right?  For example, on first and second downs.  Follow the plan, move the ball forward, and then the explosive moments will come by themselves.  I don't think you should specifically hunt for explosive moments. They arise naturally within the game plan.  So that will be my mood.  This will be our mood when we take the field. What have you seen in Emmanuel Wilson since he got a more significant role? Yes, he is wonderful, simply incredible. He's just very mature.  Perhaps that's the best way to put it—he makes the most of every day, never succumbing to excessive euphoria or disappointment.  If he is not sure about something , he always asks questions, and asks the right questions.  But yeah, I would say he's very mature, and he's a really good leader for this group. What is important in short yardage situations, especially in designed runs? Yes, I think a lot of time and effort is spent on working out these plays, and coaches know how to effectively plan such moments.  They are doing a great job in this regard. So, again, it's up to us as players to go out on the field, get the job done, and do our job.  Not just on short yards, but on every single play. You rank fourth in fourth quarter and overtime comebacks.  What is the key for a quarterback and balance in such situations? Yes, I think, first of all, it's constant training. I think we're doing a great job in Seattle. Coach Mike understands how important these situations are.  So the ability to constantly practice such moments gives us an advantage, and for me personally, it's an understanding of the situation itself.  For example, how many timeouts do we have ?  How much time is left on the clock?  What do we need to do?  Do we need a field goal?    Do we need a touchdown? It is important to take all of this into account, evaluate the options on the field, and if you don't like anything, pass to a player closer. Of course, if time allows it. Of course, there's a lot to think about, but then again , we practice so much that it becomes natural.  But yeah, I have to credit Coach Mike for how much time we put into it. How important is it that you get a little more opportunity to influence the game offensively with Brian Schottenheimer? How much does it relate to the throws you like versus the combinations you want to execute? Just curious. Yes, I think a lot of game planning depends on our coaches, who spend a lot of time watching video and analyzing what the opponent's defense has problems with or what our offense is very strong at.  So there's always a good balance between what we like to do......and what their defense has difficulty with, whether it's in coverage or in playing against carryovers.  That is, which remote game options attack them better .  So, there is a balance;  and I, you know, if we're leaning one way or the other, I just remind not only the coaches but the players, "Let's keep doing what we love and what we know from training camp and preseason." Sorry. Sam, they like to pull seven or eight players into cover.  They don't go blitzing with Raheem Morris often.  As a quarterback, what do you focus on the most when playing against a team that maximizes the number of players in coverage? Yes, I would say they are very good at diversifying their game.  You know, whether they're pulling eight or seven or, let's say, going five-man, or dropping defensive ends— Raheem and his staff are great at keeping the offense off balance, they try to play defense aggressively.  Almost the same as us.  So I think it's important for the offense, and especially for the quarterback, to understand what's causing us problems on each play, to ask questions throughout the week, and to understand where the passing options are in those schemes. Regarding the game plan, your contribution is just a few draws per week?  Is this a significant number? Yeah, I mean I like to let our coaches do their thing, I don't try to do too much.  If I see something, I say it.  If I see something wrong with the draw, or, you know, someone doesn't like something, I just talk about it, because there are no secrets in this building . You know, it's important for all of us to be able to communicate, and I try to do that every week. The extra work you do with Rashid Shahid.  I'm curious how you see this manifesting from week to week? Are you becoming more confident with him?  Yes. Yes, Sheed—he's a great guy.  It's a pleasure to work with him. I think, first of all, he's just fun to talk to.  So spending time with him is easy.  You know, it's like with all our skilled players , and with the whole team in general.  Lots of nice guys, so when we have the opportunity to discuss the route or even talk about life, we always take the chance to chat a little And what do you think about Zach, the first few days of him training with you again?  We couldn't see it.  So, what is your impression of him being with you again, at this point? He looks great. He is in great shape. It looks fresh, which it is.  Um, no, he looks really good, dude.  He, he's doing his job. When you see Nikema and Vori making playmaking moments all over the field, both in training and during the game? Yeah, I mean, he, he's causing trouble, right?  For a lot of offense, and he, uh, caused us a lot of problems in .  So I know this, uh, from my own experience, so, uh, it's nice to see him there, uh, on our team. Well, how distracting is that when trying to develop a game plan and figure everything out?  I think it requires a lot of concentration when you're building a game plan. Undoubtedly.  You know, when, when you have a guy like that who can play multiple positions and do a lot of things on the field, it makes game planning difficult. What is your vision for where the offense is now, in 4 weeks, and where you would like it to take a small step forward? Yeah, I think, you know, for us it's, you know, continuing, you know, I mean, I think, the details, it's, you know, it's something we're always chasing. Um, we always have to be more detailed, and, you know, we're always going to chase that, you know, until the very end.  Um, but I think for us too, especially for me, how about turnovers, how about the ability to protect the ball.  Um, you know, because you know, when you, when you defend the ball, you always have a chance in this league and in these games .  So, um, for me, I have to defend the ball a little better, and as an offense, I think we just have to keep chasing those details like we do I have a question about, um, communicating with the coordinator during breaks between draws.  Which, I guess, aren't conversations because they're one-sided, but what exactly do they say before they announce the actual draw? Yeah, that's, you know, that's, that's a great question, because a lot of coordinators are different.  Um, you know, and for us, as Brian and I continue to get to know each other, how much information do I really need before the draw?  Um, and for us, it's really just, you know, talking about, talking about the scrimmage that we're doing, you know, and whether there's a certain look that we're looking for, but, you know, for the most part, we discuss all of these things throughout the week. Well, in many ways, you know, when he calls out a combination, I already know exactly what he's thinking.  So, yes, of course, there are special situations, like when there's two minutes left, he's great at communicating with me, telling me what we're planning, like where the line is for a field goal, or how many yards we need to go from the 50- yard line.  So, you know, that's what we always strive for—that understanding between the offensive coordinator and the quarterback. And that always happens before the combination is called, I think, right? Yeah, so, you know, there's mostly no conversation at this point.  He just gives me the combination, but, again, on special occasions he says something. Where does he fall on the spectrum of coordinators you've had in the league—from those who talk a lot to those who are quiet or uncommunicative? Well, like I said, you know, with him...a lot of coordinators, I would say, don't talk very much. You know, the main thing is to pass on the combination on time, because time is short, and I know he thinks a lot about combination to choose, and who knows how long it takes.  So as soon as he passes the combination, we're in the game, and there's no time for much chatter .  But, of course, I would say that most coordinators, in my opinion , follow the approach of "just pass the combination" and then, as I said, special situations. Does he sometimes ask you, "Hey, do you like this option here?"  And you... Yes.  Well, I mean , there are times on the field that we can communicate like that , but I probably won't tell you all the details, but there are times when we communicate on the field, or he's trying to tell me something and I'm trying to answer him.  Let's see how long it takes for quarterbacks to have a button that allows them to communicate with the coordinator.  I'm not sure if many coordinators would be thrilled about that, but, you know, maybe it's in store for us in the future.  The 49ers use stunts more often than any other defense.  How much attention do you pay to that , rather than just leaving it up to Jaylen and the line? Yeah, I mean, it's always, you know, working with the stunners and the defensive line—that's something our offensive line does really well throughout the week. That's something I can't really worry about as a quarterback.  But again , that's a credit to their defense— forcing offenses to play "second and long," those run- back situations, " third and long," where they can use their stunts and get more people into coverage. What do you like about Rasheed when he comes out of the backfield? Yeah, I mean, he's just a weapon, like Nick, you know, in our defense.  He is a player who can be put in a multitude of positions and used in a variety of ways. How do you think the defense is responding to this? After all, Jackson also played a lot out of the backfield, running routes and so on.  And how do you think the defense changes when one of these guys is there instead of a running back? their business, right?  That is, do they want to do a check, or have combinations prepared, or act in a certain way when he is there;  but, in the end, we have a plan for everything, and we act accordingly. Okay, thanks, Zach. Yes, guys, thank you.  Thank you.
